Title: Identification to Subclasses of Chordal Graphs
Text:
Identification to Subclasses of Chordal Graphs∗
Petr A. Golovach†
Laure Morelle†
Daniël Paulusma‡
Abstract
An identification of two vertices u and v in a graph replaces them with a new vertex whose neighborhood
is the union of the neighborhoods of u and v. We study the H-Identification problem, which is to
decide whether a given graph G can be transformed (“identified”) to a graph in H by applying at most
k vertex identifications. We determine the classical and parameterized complexity of this problem for
various subclasses H of chordal graphs, obtaining an almost complete picture for two parameters: k and
n −k. We also consider the Identification problem, which is to test for two given graphs G and H if G
can be identified to H. We determine the parameterized complexity of this problem when H is a graph
from one of our testbed classes, taking the number of simplicial vertices of H as the parameter.

Introduction
An identification of two vertices u and v in a graph G replaces u and v with a new vertex wuv made adjacent
to all neighbors of both u and v (equivalently, one may first add an edge between u and v if it is not already
present, and then contract this edge). For a fixed class of graphs H, we define the problem H-Identification.
The input consists of a graph G and an integer k, and the question is whether G can be transformed into some
graph H ∈H using at most k identifications. We study the parameterized complexity of H-Identification
and provide a comprehensive complexity analysis for well-known subclasses H of chordal graphs.
The H-Identification problem falls within the framework of graph modification problems, where
the goal is to decide whether a given graph can be modified into a graph in a class H using at most k
operations from some specific set S of allowed modifications. For example, if S consists of vertex deletion,
edge deletion, and edge contraction, then we obtain the H-Minor problem. Another well-known variant
related to H-Identification is H-Contraction, for which S consists solely of edge contraction.
Most graph modification problems are NP-complete and have been extensively studied from the perspective
of parameterized complexity. For example, if H is minor-closed, such as forests, series-parallel graphs,
planar graphs, and graphs of bounded treewidth, then, for fixed k, the yes-instances of both H-Minor
and H-Identification form a minor-closed graph class as well. Hence, both problems can be solved in
f(k, H) · n1+o(1) time [20, 26] (see also [15, 23]). This argument does not hold for H-Contraction [23] (see
e.g. [14, 16, 17, 18]).
If the graphs in H have treewidth at most p and can be characterized in CMSO logic, such as forests,
and outerplanar graphs, then the same holds for the class of yes-instances of H-Identification. Hence,
Courcelle’s Theorem [1, 5] yields an g(p, k) · n time algorithm.
However, when H is not minor-closed or does not have bounded treewidth, not much is known except for
the case when H = {H} for some single graph H. In this case, we simply write H-Identification and note

Classifying the complexity of H∗-Compaction is still open; see also the survey [2]. However, Vikas

but in XP when parameterized by |V (H)| if H is chordal [29]; a graph is chordal if it has no induced cycle on
four or more vertices. This result for H-Identification is tight in the sense that even K1,ℓ-Identification
is W[1]-hard when parameterized by ℓ, where K1,ℓdenotes the star on ℓ+ 1 vertices (which is chordal).

What is the parameterized complexity of H-Identification beyond the case H = {H}, when H ranges over
classes of chordal graphs?
Note that both the input graph G and the fixed graph H in H-Identification are irreflexive.
Our Results. We use the following subclasses of chordal graphs as testbeds for our study: paths, linear
forests, stars, trees, forests, complete graphs, clusters, split graphs, interval graphs and chordal graphs. Note
that forests have treewidth at most 1, implying that H-Identification can be solved in g(k) · n time via
meta-theorems [1, 5] if H is any subclass of forests, as observed earlier. In these cases, we still aim for a
stronger result. All our other testbed classes H have unbounded treewidth and are not minor-closed, and
therefore, none of the previous meta-theorems [1, 5, 20, 23, 26] apply.

Identification to Acyclic Graphs
In this section, we consider H-Identification for the cases when H is a class of stars, trees, or forests. We
refer to those problems as Star-Identification, Tree-Identification, and Forest-Identification,
respectively.
3.1
Algorithmic Lower Bounds
We start with establishing hardness results for H-Identification where H is a class of acyclic graphs.
Theorem 1. Let H be the class of stars, trees, or forests. Then H-Identification is NP-complete and
W[1]-hard parameterized by n −k.
Proof. We reduce from Independent Set. The Independent Set problem asks, given a graph G and a
positive integer p, whether G has an independent set of size at least p. Independent Set is well-known
to be NP-complete [12] and W[1]-complete when parameterized by the solution size p [11]. Let (G, p) be an
instance of Independent Set for p ≥2. Denote by G′ the graph obtained from G by adding a universal
vertex u (cf. Figure 2). We claim that G has an independent set I of size p if and only if (G′, n −(p + 1)) is
a yes-instance of H-Identification.

3.2
Kernelization for Identification to Acyclic Graphs
In this section, we investigate the parameterized complexity of H-Identification parameterized by k for
the cases when H is the class of stars, trees, or forests. We show that in all these cases, H-Identification
admits a polynomial kernel when parameterized by k.
For stars, we observe that the problem is equivalent to Vertex Cover. We remind that the task of the
Vertex Cover problem is to decide, given a graph G and a non-negative integer k, whether G has a vertex
cover of size at most k.
Observation 2. Let G be a graph with p isolated vertices, and let k ≥0 be an integer. Then G has a vertex
cover of size at most k if and only if G admits an identification to a star by at most p + k −1 identifications.

Proof. The claim is trivial if G has no edges. Assume from now on that this is not the case.
Let X be a vertex cover of size at most k. As G has an edge, X ̸= ∅. We identify the vertices of X
into a single vertex, and then identify this vertex with the p isolated vertices of the original graph. It is
straightforward to see that the resulting graph is a star obtained by |X| −1 + p ≤p + k −1 identifications.
For the opposite direction, assume that a star S is an identification of G obtained by at most p + k −1
identifications. Denote by c the center vertex of S. Let W = {W(x) | x ∈V (S)} be an S-witness structure.

completes the proof.

Future Work
We presented a comprehensive study of the complexity of H-Identification and Identification for ten
well-known classes of chordal graphs, including the class of chordal graphs themselves. Our results are
summarized in Tables 1 and 2. By using a systematic approach, we were able to identify two open problems:
Is H-Identification, parameterized by k, FPT or W[1]-hard when H is the class of interval graphs or the
class of chordal graphs?
It is also possible to consider alternative parameters. For example, we may ask whether a given graph
G can be modified into a graph from a specified class H by involving at most p vertices in a sequence of
identifications. This variant was studied in [24], where a polynomial kernel was obtained when H is the class
of forests (through a reduction to Vertex Cover). Since k identifications involve p ≤2k vertices, this result
yields an FPT 2-approximation algorithm for H-Identification.
Finally, we recall that for the minor relation, the set of permitted graph operations consists of vertex
deletion, edge deletion and edge contraction. If we only allow vertex deletion and edge contraction, then we
obtain the induced minor relation. In both relations we could replace edge contraction by vertex identification.
In the first case, we obtain the identification minor relation. This containment relation was introduced in [24].
We name the second case as induced identification minor.
We note that the corresponding decision problems H-Identification Minor and H-Induced Iden-
tification Minor are in XP, when parameterized by |V (H)|. This can be seen as follows. For each edge
xy ∈E(H), we guess an edge uv ∈E(G) where we place u in W(x) and v in W(y). We also guess a vertex t
of G to be in a bag W(z) for each isolated vertex z ∈V (H). We assign the set R of all non-guessed vertices to
an arbitrary bag. For the variant H-Identification Minor, we delete all edges incident to R and between
vertices of bags that must be non-adjacent. For the variant H-Induced Identification Minor, we simply
delete all vertices of R. We now identify each bag to a single vertex. If we do not obtain H (which may
happen when edge deletions are not allowed), then we discard the branch and try again.
We leave a more extensive complexity study of H-Identification Minor and H-Induced Identi-
fication Minor for future work. As a final remark, we note that the identification minor relation is
well-quasi-ordered [24], which implies that every identification-minor-closed graph class admits a finite
obstruction set. In contrast, this does not hold for the induced identification minor relation: for example, the
complements of cycles form an infinite antichain (see also [24] for another infinite antichain).

Abstract: An identification of two vertices u and v in a graph replaces them with a new vertex whose neighborhood is the union of the neighborhoods of u and v. We study the H-Identification problem, which is to decide whether a given graph G can be transformed (“identified”) to a graph in H by applying at most k vertex identifications. We determine the classical and parameterized complexity of this problem for various subclasses H of chordal graphs, obtaining an almost complete picture for two parameters: k and n −k. We also consider the Identification problem, which is to test for two given graphs G and H if G can be identified to H. We determine the parameterized complexity of this problem when H is a graph from one of our testbed classes, taking the number of simplicial vertices of H as the parameter.
